hypothesis: Names breaking their first 15-minute high on heavy relative volume keep going into the late morning. Written before any run; the published version of this idea reports a gross edge, so the question is whether it survives spread and slippage.
name: Opening-range breakout, stocks in play

hypothesis: A liquid large cap that opens more than 1% below yesterday's close, in a thin pre-market after overnight order imbalance, retraces part of that gap during the first two hours as the regular session's deeper liquidity arrives. The cost is a fixed few bps while a 1%+ gap leaves far more room to be recovered, so net-of-cost edge is plausible where it was not for breakouts. Written before any run. If the gap-ups and gap-downs that carry real news dominate, this loses and the stop (1.5%) is what limits it.
name: Gap-down fade, large caps

hypothesis: Execution desks benchmarked to VWAP buy when a stock trades well under it, pulling price back toward VWAP later in the day. Costs are fixed in bps, so only a deep (1.2%) stretch below VWAP, after the first hour, leaves enough expected reversion to clear them; shallow stretches (the usual setting) cannot. The target is about the size of the stretch. Written before any run. Expected to fail if a stock far below VWAP is mostly a stock with news, which trends rather than reverts.
name: VWAP reversion, deep stretches only

hypothesis: The daily RSI(2) reversion rule on AMZN and AAPL measured +117 to +150 bps a trade (t above 5) because short-term overshoots in liquid names are partly given back. The same overshoot on 15-minute bars, bought only while price is above a two-day average, may give back too, with fewer and less noisy bars than 5-minute data. Written before any run. This is the idea with the most outside support and the least reason to think intraday spreads allow it; a gross edge that costs erase is the likely result.
name: Intraday RSI(2) reversion, 15-minute bars

hypothesis: Large institutional parent orders on exceptional-volume days (opening-range volume 3x its 20-day norm) are worked across the whole session, so a break of the first 30-minute high on such a day keeps drifting into the close. The earlier ORB test failed because a 0.6% stop and 1.2% target made it a coin flip charged 5.5 bps a trade; this one trades rarely, holds to the close with a wide stop and a target that is rarely hit, so cost is small against the move. Written before any run. Expected to fail if breakouts on heavy-volume days mean-revert by the afternoon as liquidity providers reload, or if gross stays about zero as in the first ORB.
name: ORB trend day, hold to close

hypothesis: A 3%+ overnight gap down in a top-50 dollar-volume name is mostly forced selling and thin pre-market liquidity, and part of it is bought back through the day as deeper liquidity arrives. At 3% the recoverable move is several times the 5-6 bps round-trip cost, and the trade is rare. The earlier 1% gap fade had gross -1.1 bps, so this is a bet that only the extreme tail overreacts. Written before any run. Expected to fail if 3% gaps in large caps are almost all news (earnings, guidance), which drifts further down: the stop at 3% then dominates.
name: Large gap-down, hold to close

hypothesis: The 1% gap fade (gross -1.1 bps) and the deep VWAP stretch (losses concentrated on market-wide down days, where many names fall together) failed because a gap in many stocks at once is macro news that keeps going. A 1.5% gap in one large cap while the universe's median gap is within 0.3% is more likely an overnight order imbalance in a thin pre-market than information, so the retracement as regular-session liquidity arrives should be larger and independent across names. Written before any run. Expected to fail if single-name gaps of that size are mostly earnings and guidance, which drift on rather than revert; then the 1.5% stop dominates, as before.
name: Idiosyncratic gap-down fade, flat market days
